UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                            )                 Docket No. ER26-247-000
                                                      )

                         COMMENTS OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED

         Advanced Energy United (“United”) 1 submits these comments in response to the

Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) October 24, 2025, filing of Tariff Revisions to add the

High Impact Large Load (“HILL”) Processes and High Impact Large Load Generation

Assessment (“HILLGA”)2 to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”).3 The

HILL/HILLGA Filing proposes provisions to define large loads and enhance the process for

integrating HILLs onto SPP’s system. The stakeholder-supported HILL/HILLGA Filing is a

reasonable starting point to address the challenges of large load interconnections and should be

approved as just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. United looks

forward to continuing to work with SPP and the Commission to further refine and improve large

load interconnection procedures and rules for associated generation through the SPP stakeholder

process, in the Commission’s newly opened rulemaking proceeding on large load

interconnections (RM26-4-000), and in other dockets and venues as appropriate.




1
  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure,
clean and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents
the full range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy
includes energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and
more. The comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not
represent the views of any particular member.
2
  Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Tariff Revisions to Add the High Impact Large Load Processes and High Impact
Large Load Generation Assessment, Submitted in Docket No. ER26-247, (October 24, 2025) (“HILL/HILLGA
Filing”).
3
  Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Open Access Transmission Tariff, Sixth Revised Volume No. 1. References in this
filing to “Tariff” refer to the version of SPP’s Tariff currently in effect.
 I.     BACKGROUND

       In May 2025, the Board directed staff to create a framework to speed up the connection

of generation to support specific new loads. 4 SPP staff responded with the HILL proposal,

comprised of integrated design, study, registration and operations. SPP sought to create a 90-day

connection process with flexible options while minimizing impacts to non-large load customers.

Processes under the current rules to interconnect loads and generation face long wait times and

limited options without existing generation. This led staff to define a HILL as any commercial or

industrial individual load facility or aggregation of load facilities at a single site connected

through one or more shared points of interconnection or points of delivery that can pose

reliability risks to the grid. Originally, new processes for adding a HILL also included

components for a Conditional High Impact Large Load (“CHILL”), the portion of a HILL

willing to be curtailable in the longer term, but the HILL/HILLGA Filing requires a generator to

seek firm transmission service within 5 years.

       After introducing new integration processes at the July 1 Large Load Forum, staff sought

to advance the proposal quickly, outside of the normal stakeholder process. At the July Market

Operations Policy Committee (“MOPC”) meeting, stakeholders heard about three pathways for

generation projects located behind a common bus, a larger local area, or within the same

deliverability area as the HILL.5 Stakeholders raised concerns with the last option, HILLGA Path

3, which would have granted generation projects priority above other customers in the

interconnection queue without similar locational guardrails. Given its use of deliverability area

as the geographic constraint, and considering that SPP has five deliverability areas overall, this

 could have opened up the HILLGA process for generation and load pairs located much farther

from each other, creating concerns that the disconnect in location could exacerbate congestion.

The large load proposal presented at the July MOPC failed when put to a vote, with only 53.73%

approval.6 At a special MOPC in August, staff presented the scaled-back version of its HILLS

proposal, which removed HILLGA Path 3 and severed the CHIILLS policy for future

consideration via a separate stakeholder process7. With additional time for CHILLS review and

removal of the HILLGA Pathway 3, stakeholders approved the HILL proposal with 95%

approval.8 The Board gave its support on September 4. 9

II.     COMMENTS

      A. HILL/HILLGA STUDY PROCESSES ARE JUST AND REASONABLE AND NOT
         UNDULY DISCRIMINATORY

        SPP rightly recognizes that there are unique challenges in accommodating large loads due

to their operational characteristics and reliability needs. In addition to these lasting

characteristics, there is also an upfront timing mismatch, with large loads able to come online

faster than new generation and transmission upgrades.10 The HILL/HILLGA Filing proposes a

study process and operations framework that rewards flexibility while maintaining guardrails to

protect the reliability of the SPP system and the integrity of the regular generator interconnection

queue. As described in the filing, the HILL and HILLGA constructs will allow SPP to

 “incorporate large loads into SPP in a reliable manner” while also introducing “an optional

process for studying the limited interconnection of generating resources identified specifically to

serve large loads.”11 The HILL/HILLGA Filing will define large loads and create a new pathway

for a HILL and its associated generation or storage resources to connect while ensuring adequate

guardrails on the system to preserve reliability and insulate other interconnection customers. The

HILL/HILLGA Filing balances costs for ratepayers to protect customers while offering a flexible

path to interconnect new loads and options for studying generation co-located with those new

loads. This addresses the need for speed while insulating customers from rate impacts and

ensuring affordability is not affected. To minimize repercussions on other customers, the

proposed HILLGA process studies supply and demand collectively, ensuring load will pay for

their costs, while encouraging flexibility in a framework that accelerates the overall timeline for

interconnection.

       1. The HILL Process Appropriately Addresses the Unique Characteristics of Large
          Loads Entering the SPP System

           SPP defines a HILL as a “new commercial or industrial load, or increase in commercial

or industrial load, at a single site connected through one or more shared Points of Interconnection

(POIs) or delivery points” and sets two size thresholds for the definition of a HILL: greater than

or equal to 10 MW if connected below 69 kV, and greater than or equal to 50 MW if connected

above 69 kV.”12 The filing outlines additional requirements for the study of HILLs to evaluate

the impact of the load on the transmission system and ensure the transmission customer has




11
     HILL/HILLGA Filing, SPP Transmittal Letter at 4.
12
     HILL/HILLGA Filing, SPP Transmittal Letter at 12.
 sufficient resources to meet any existing load plus the new HILL, 13 including additional study

deposits and application fees14 and ongoing operational requirements.15

         The process to connect a HILL appropriately recognizes the different characteristics and

needs of new large loads, and the requirements placed on HILLs flow directly from those

characteristics. Specifically, the HILL process ensures that the potential impact of new large

loads on the system is adequately studied, and then imposes requirements to avoid any adverse

reliability impacts once they are connected, by increasing visibility and operational safeguards.

The additional studies include reliability impacts using transient stability assessments, system

strength screening, and Electromagnetic Transient if necessary, as well as requiring a HILL

Delivery Point Study, which is a “more rigorous set of analyses than would typically apply under

Attachment AQ or Attachment AX.”16 Beyond these evaluations, SPP will also require higher

application fees, study deposits, and financial surety requirements above what is typically

applied.17 These additional requirements will prevent speculative projects and ensure only

shovel-ready projects enter this process while requiring that HILLs cover all applicable study

costs.

         SPP drew heavily from ongoing discussions of the NERC Large Load Task Force and

adapted these to meet the needs of its system. When setting the threshold for loads subject to the

more stringent HILLs process, SPP relied on NERC surveys and the actual impact that loads of

different sizes have on the transmission system at different voltages. 18 The heightened scrutiny,

 increased study costs, and operational requirements for HILLs are not unduly discriminatory

because they are derived from and responsive to the impact these loads have on the system.

           While the HILL proposal is a good starting point, United encourages SPP and the

Commission to continue to refine and iterate its study processes and requirements for HILLs as

best practices evolve. Additional information and input on these topics will be fleshed out in the

Commission’s ongoing proceeding in RM26-4-000 addressing large load additions, which may

uncover opportunities to refine or improve the HILLS process. Nonetheless, SPP has met its

burden to demonstrate that the HILLs process as filed is just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory, and the Commission should approve it.

       2. The New HILLGA Process Addresses the Need for New Generation to Serve Large
          Loads While Ensuring Sufficient Guardrails to Avoid Undue Discrimination

           The HILL/HILLGA Filing also creates a new transmission service option and an

expedited pathway for limited connection of generation to serve a HILL 19 through its “optional

HILLGA process to facilitate the prompt interconnection of generating Resources that are

specifically identified for and limited to serving a HILL.” 20 The HILLGA pathway complements

the requirement in the HILL process that the transmission customer must have sufficient

resources to meet existing load and the new HILL, by creating a pathway for the HILL to bring

online new generation to serve any new load that exceeds available resources. The HILLGA

process differs from the regular generator interconnection process in that requests can be

submitted anytime, so participants do not need to wait for a new cycle application window to

open. Crucially, the HILLGA process includes important guardrails to avoid impacting the

Definitive Interconnect System Impact Studies (“DISIS”) queue or granting undue preference to



19
     HILL/HILLGA Filing, SPP Transmittal Letter at 11.
20
     HILL/HILLGA Filing, SPP Transmittal Letter at 23.
 generation or storage proceeding through the HILLGA pathway. HILLGA is designed as an

interconnection pathway solely to enable a new resource to serve a specific HILL. Several

elements of the HILLGA proposal render it just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory.

           First, the HILLGA process does not confer full interconnection service—that is reserved

for resources processed through the standard interconnection process. Instead, the filing

“establishes another new option for transmission connection through its Load Limited Resource

Interconnection Service (“LLRIS”)” that gives the new generating unit “injection rights limited

to the HILL, which it is supporting.”21 Resources connecting via the HILLGA construct alone

will not be granted Network Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”) or Energy Resource

Interconnection Service (“ERIS”) transmission service unless they apply through the standard

interconnection process.22 By requiring that generation seek transmission service through the

regular DISIS process, the HILLGA proposal ensures that no resources receive preferential

treatment. However, this could result in stranded assets if the load fails to materialize or ceases

operations, or if the generator is able to successfully navigate the DISIS queue and receive

transmission service after the five-year requirement. SPP should monitor use of the HILLGA

pathway and assess whether additional reforms are needed to address potential inefficiencies

resulting from this two-track approach. However, its inclusion in the initial filing is critical to

avoid potential undue discrimination or preference.

           Second, HILLGA also has more stringent application requirements than the DISIS

process. These include higher application fees, tiers of study deposits, a higher financial security

deposit, identification of a Point of Interconnection (“POI”), as well as demonstration of meeting




21
     HILL/HILLGA Filing, SPP Transmittal Letter at 23.
22
     HILL/HILLGA Filing, SPP Transmittal Letter at 23.
 milestones and site control.23 The financial commitments are double the requirements in the

DISIS process, and non-financial milestones are in excess of what is required at the equivalent

stage of the DISIS process. These requirements will ensure that generation paired with the HILL

will show up, and reduce speculative applications.

        Third, SPP’s geographic requirements also minimize impacts by requiring the

identification of the POI for the proposed generating resource and requiring it to be in close

electrical proximity in the same area to the load, defined as “no more than two substations away

from the HILL.”24 By studying the local impacts and requiring that the generation only serve the

HILL, this process aims to reduce withdrawals that cause additional restudies. 25 The

HILL/HILLGA Filing links the generating facility with the HILL, ensuring upgrade costs are

associated with that project, rather than passed on to other customers. These geographic

limitations will lead to fewer triggered upgrades and minimal impacts on other interconnection

requests, while also minimizing congestion that could have broader adverse impacts.

        Finally, SPP is proposing to treat HILLGA Requests as existing generators when

including them in its transmission planning models, meaning they “will not appear in Definitive

Interconnection System Impact Study (“DISIS”) studies until the DISIS models have been

updated to new ITP models and therefore cannot drive upgrade costs or restudies for those DISIS

clusters.”26 This will also minimize the cost impacts on customers.

        As with the HILL component of the proposal, United encourages SPP and the

Commission to continue to refine and iterate the HILLGA process as SPP gains experience with

HILLGA and as best practices evolve. Additional information and input on these topics will be

 brought to the Commission in the RM26-4-000 proceeding addressing large load additions,

which may uncover opportunities to further improve the HILLGA process to achieve the goal of

speed to power for new large loads while avoiding undue discrimination and ensuring just and

reasonable rates for all customers.

       CONCLUSION

       SPP’s proposal is a just and reasonable solution to the growing concerns over bringing on

new large loads while ensuring resource adequacy and reliability needs are met. SPP’s proposed

changes to the Tariff enable new resources bringing their own generation to be interconnected to

the transmission system quickly and efficiently allowing for faster interconnection with

guardrails limiting the impact on the system and other customers. Advanced Energy United

respectfully requests that the Commission accept SPP’s HILLS/HILLGA Filing as proposed.
